question: to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE) Subject:

Romania, an EU Member State since 2007, is once again in the throes of a deep political crisis. A government is not expected to be formed before September, and the country is failing to implement the reforms required to access approximately EUR 5.1 billion in recovery funds. Almost twenty years after accession, Romania is still grappling with political instability, weak institutions and corruption. Membership has not resolved these problems, but has instead imported them into the Union, whilst at the same time recovery funds are being paid for by EU taxpayers. Nevertheless, the Commission is pressing ahead with negotiations with Moldova: following the opening of the first cluster on 15 June 2026, it intends to open all remaining clusters before the summer recess. However, Moldova’s institutional and economic situation is even worse than Romania’s was at the same point in time. The following questions thus arise: 1.
How does the Commission assess its enlargement policy, given the ongoing governance and institutional problems in Romania twenty years after accession?
On the basis of which criteria does the Commission conclude that Moldova meets the Copenhagen criteria and does not pose comparable risks to the Union’s absorption capacity?

Is the Commission prepared to suspend accession negotiations until it has been demonstrated that further enlargement will not entail any new administrative, institutional or financial risks for the Union and its taxpayers? If not, why not?
answer: (English version) to the Commission Mieke Andriese (PfE) (7 July 2026) Subject: Developments in Romania as a precedent for halting further EU enlargement Romania, an EU Member State since 2007, is once again in the throes of a deep political crisis. A government is not expected to be formed before September, and the country is failing to implement the reforms required to access approximately EUR 5.1 billion in recovery funds. Almost twenty years after accession, Romania is still grappling with political instability, weak institutions and corruption. Membership has not resolved these problems, but has instead imported them into the Union, whilst at the same time recovery funds are being paid for by EU taxpayers. Nevertheless, the Commission is pressing ahead with negotiations with Moldova: following the opening of the first cluster on 15 June 2026, it intends to open all remaining clusters before the summer recess. However, Moldova’s institutional and economic situation is even worse than Romania’s was at the same point in time. The following questions thus arise: 1.
How does the Commission assess its enlargement policy, given the ongoing governance and institutional problems in Romania twenty years after accession?
On the basis of which criteria does the Commission conclude that Moldova meets the Copenhagen criteria and does not pose comparable risks to the Union’s absorption capacity?

Is the Commission prepared to suspend accession negotiations until it has been demonstrated that further enlargement will not entail any new administrative, institutional or financial risks for the Union and its taxpayers? If not, why not?

(19 August 2026) EU enlargement policy is guided by a merit-based process and the assessment of any candidate country, including Moldova, is based on its own progress in delivering the required reforms, particularly on the so-called ‘fundamentals’ — democracy, the rule of law, fundamental rights, public administration reform and the economic criteria — in line with the 2020 revised enlargement methodology (1). This framework provides for continuous monitoring and allows for reversibility where progress stalls or backsliding occurs. This ensures that negotiations remain closely linked to tangible and sustained reform outcomes. To ensure that new Member States continue to safeguard and maintain their track-record on the rule of law, democracy and fundamental rights, the Commission considers that future Accession Treaties should contain stronger safeguards against backsliding on commitments made during the accession negotiations. Enlargement will continue to advance based on the pace of reforms in candidate countries while taking into account the EU’s capacity to integrate new members effectively. The Commission is currently preparing pre-enlargement policy reviews, to be presented in the autumn, as part of the EU’s wider work to ensure that the EU is politically, institutionally and financially prepared for a larger membership.

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions: Enhancing the Accession Process — A Credible EU Perspective for the Western Balkans, COM(2020) 57 final, Brussels, 5 February 2020.
